chunks: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who takes his father, or his mother, or his brother, or his sister as slaves. So he said: 'As for the sister, she is emancipated the moment he owns her; and as for the brother, he may enslave him; and as for the two parents, they are both emancipated the moment he owns them both.'

He (the narrator) said: And I asked him about the woman who breastfeeds her slave — can she take him as a slave? He said: 'She emancipates him, and it is an abhorrence (for her to breastfeed her slave).'

key_terms.عَتَقَتْ / عَتَقَا: Emancipated/freed — automatic legal freedom conferred by ownership of close kin
key_terms.كَارِهَةٌ: Averse, disliking — indicating the act of breastfeeding one's slave is considered reprehensible (makruh) or forbidden
key_terms.يَسْتَرِقُّهُ: To enslave — the permissibility of keeping a brother as a slave
key_terms.يَمْلِكُهَا / يَمْلِكُهُمَا: To own/possess — the moment of ownership triggers automatic emancipation

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling in Shia Islam on a man who comes to own his parents or sister as slaves?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) addresses the legal ruling on a Muslim man who comes to own close family members as slaves — a scenario that could arise from war, debt, or purchase in the slave economies of classical Islamic civilization. The Imam rules that parents and sisters are automatically emancipated upon ownership, while a brother may remain enslaved. A second ruling addresses the case of a woman who breastfeeds her male slave, establishing that this act of nursing creates a milk-kinship bond (rida'a) that necessitates his emancipation, though the act itself is considered abhorrent. These rulings reflect the Shia jurisprudential tradition of limiting and ultimately dissolving slavery within certain family and kinship relationships.
